utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Let me first introduce to you why the Chamber wanted to have this Status Conference. I provided you with a copy of a document I prepared, Data, Analysis, and Extrapolation of the Time Used for Examination of Witnesses in the Galic Case. Of course, this was drafted after five witnesses, and I must say that the parties have improved since then, but nevertheless, the Chamber is not confident that this is forever. What you see on this document is that I listed the time, the estimated time for the five witnesses, and also how much time had been used, which is 25 per cent more than the estimate was. And then in cross-examination, the Defence took even 10 per cent more compared to the time used by the Prosecution. So therefore, an average time for each witness of six and a half hours and the estimate of the Prosecution -- just -- these are rough figures, they're not precise figures, as you'll understand. 150 witnesses viva voce, that would take 975 hours. One day in court, I find out, never gives more than four hours of examination. Usually the time we've got is four and three quarters of an hour, and of course, the breaks go off. So that would be 244 days in court. Every month 22 days, that means 18 -- 13 months. Then since we started, we had the winter recess, we'll have the summer recess, we'll have the winter recess in 2002 as well. We'll stay an additional two weeks in recess during the year. That would mean an extra 11 weeks. So the Prosecution case, if we do not speed up, would be completed by the end of March 2003, and then we're not even talking about calling any additional 92 bis witnesses. I thought it wise to confront the parties with the situation. Of course, at this moment, it's mainly the Prosecution, but you can be sure that the Defence will face similar problems if it comes to the presentation of their case. I wanted to confront you with this situation and then I'd like to invite you to give any suggestions for speeding up. So I would first hear from the Prosecution, because this must have been in their minds as well, and if not, at least during the last half hour, what suggestions they have. Because we want to listen to the parties but will not hesitate to do it otherwise if the parties are not able to speed up. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Firstly, in relation to the figures that you have provided to us before the break, I think they can be updated. The first five witnesses that the Prosecution has called are indicated on the sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If one adds to those names the names and details of the last two witnesses, whose evidence is completed, we have Milovanovic, in respect of whom there was an estimate of one and a half hours. On my calculations, his evidence-in-chief, in fact, took one hour and six minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I told, that you have improved considerably. I'm aware of that, and to that extent, it's not totally fair what I did write down. But let's keep to the main lines. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. There's a reason why I say this, Mr. President. And the seventh witness was Mr. Hajir. We gave an estimate of two hours and we took three quarters of an hour. Now, that means that our estimate for the seven witnesses totals 16 hours and the time actually taken in chief was 17 hours. We're one hour out, after seven witnesses and 17 hours of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The discrepancy for the Defence is greater. I simply make that observation. I'll come back to it. I appreciate that these figures indicate that something drastic must be done. I have some proposals. And indeed, the Prosecution put into place one of those proposals this morning, in particular, in relation to the manner in which we dealt with Dr. Hajir. I'll come back to that. I make this observation in relation to the evidence given by the seven witnesses so far: There has not been one dispute put to any of those witnesses in relation to any aspect of their evidence during

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: required, since they are the cross-examining party, to put to a witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness. Having regard to the Defence pre-trial brief, where does that -- what does that leave one to conclude? In essence, the pre-trial brief filed by the Defence I think could safely be summarised as being to the effect that the sniping and shelling of civilians by forces under the command or control of the accused did not take place, but if it did, then he was not aware of it. I appreciate that's perhaps an oversimplification, but it will do for the purposes of my argument. It seems, therefore, that none of the evidence which this Tribunal has thus far heard in this case is contrary to the Defence of the accused. In other words, for instance, in relation to clear first-hand evidence that we have so far heard, in particular from Mr. Ashton, of deliberate sniping and shelling of civilians by Romanija Corps soldiers, it seems that that evidence is not disputed. It would follow that the Defence must be relying upon the second aspect as set out in their pre-trial brief, that is: If it happened, we accept it happened, but the accused did not know of it. When one turns from the witness -- the evidence we have so far heard and contemplates another year of Prosecution evidence, much of which will involve similar accounts, it seems to me that one course we could take is that witnesses for the Prosecution, by agreement, read parts of their witness statements during their evidence in chief. I propose that the parts of the statements that be read, and therefore be given by way of sworn evidence before the Tribunal, be those parts in relation to which the Defence effectively says: We don't dispute that that happened, but the accused did not know about it. To give Your Honours an example, many of the witnesses the Prosecution will call in relation to scheduled sniping incidents will also give evidence, not only about the scheduled incident but about their awareness of many other incidents of sniping and shelling of civilians, of individuals they knew, or in some cases, incidents which happened to them. That is evidence of a type which is the same as the evidence given by John Ashton and during which at no stage was it said to him: You're lying when you say that you saw civilians being shelled from the other side of the confrontation line. At no stage was it put to him: You are mistaken when you say that you saw civilians shelled or sniped from the other side of the confrontation line. To continue with my example, because of the central significance of the scheduled incidents, in particular, since they form part of the indictment, those witnesses could still give evidence in the traditional way in relation to the actual scheduled incident but then could be taken to the balance of their statement insofar as it relates to unscheduled incidents and simply invited to read those portions. That would save a lot of time. The same could be applied to scheduled shelling incident witnesses; that evidence which falls into the same category could be read. And if one adopts this approach, then there are other types of evidence which could be given in that way, that is, evidence which the Defence does not intend to put to the witness "You're lying" or "You're mistaken." That is my first proposal. My second proposal relates to something which Your Honours would have observed this morning during the examination-in-chief of Dr. Hajir. That is that the Prosecution deliberately led the witness to the relevant parts of his testimony. Leading questions were used on what might be regarded as non-contentious aspects of his testimony. And when the witness finally arrived at the relevant part, then the Prosecution stopped using leading questions and fell back into questions in a normal form. Now, this is a technique which is widely used in common-law trials, that where there is no real dispute, it's permissible, subject to the Defence right to object, in order to save time, to get the witness as quickly as possible to the relevant part. Your Honours would have noticed during this morning's evidence, and during the evidence on previous days, that quite often the witness will give an answer that one might think is unduly lengthy, and the Prosecution proposes that, when this occurs in future, to interrupt the witness and redirect the witness to the relevant aspect of the evidence. Your Honours, a central difficulty for the Prosecution at this stage of the presentation of its case has been that it has been unclear from the way in which cross-examination has occurred precisely what is in dispute. The reason that we need to know that is, for instance, if it becomes clear that an aspect of the Prosecution case is not in dispute, then we can safely abandon calling future witnesses whose evidence would corroborate the evidence which has already been heard and which is now not in dispute. Unless there is a clear understanding that certain areas are not in dispute, then we cannot, as a matter of fairness to ourselves, to the Prosecution, abandon corroborative evidence. I will give an example from the evidence of John Ashton. As I've already indicated, in spite of six hours of cross-examination, not once was it put to him that he was untruthful or mistaken in relation to any aspect of his evidence, and yet, at the conclusion of his evidence, the Defence successfully, as it turned out, tendered his previous statements. The Defence was challenged by the Prosecution as to the relevance of the tendering of those statements, and their explanation was that it went to his credibility. Credibility can only arise as an issue if there is something in the witness's evidence which the Defence does not accept. If his evidence is entirely accepted, then there can be no issue of credibility. One then ponders: Well, what was it that he said which was not accepted by the Defence when they did not put to him any aspect of his evidence as being disputed. So I think there needs to be a clear understanding in the Trial Chamber that Rule 90 applies and that it is in the interests of an efficient trial that if something is in dispute, it be fairly put to the witness in accordance with Rule 90. To give another brief example, John Ashton was shown a number of photographs of tanks. He was asked to identify each tank. It was not suggested to him at the conclusion of that exercise that he had made any mistake. Is the Prosecution entitled to presume that there will be no dispute as to his identification of the tanks? Because if there is to be such a dispute, it was not put to him. It was not said to him that his identification of a particular tank was wrong, that in fact it was a different type of tank. This is the type of issue upon which there has to be a clear understanding, if there is to be an efficient trial. I move on to my second point again. The Prosecution proposes that, in the same way as it has now started to streamline its evidence around the principle of relevance, the Defence should do likewise. There have been some witnesses that the Prosecution has called and the Defence has cross-examined for hours, and much of that cross-examination, I suggest to Your Honours, is lacking in any apparent relevance whatsoever. One might think that the attitude of the Defence is that if they are allowed a particular amount of time to cross-examine, then there is a feeling they must use up all of that time. In early December, I anticipated to Your Honours that after the break, after Christmas, the Christmas break, I would propose that the time limits be reconsidered and the guiding principle instead, rather than a set amount of time, be simply relevance. If one applies that to the witnesses that the Prosecution has called --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, if I may interrupt you. Unfortunately, we have three quarters of an hour. You might say that I have not planned enough time, but you took almost half of it, and so if there are any other points you would like to raise. Because it's quite clear to us here, Rule 90 relevance, you made three proposals in order to speed up your examination for witnesses. Are there other specific issues or suggestions you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In the interests of time, Mr. President, I will leave it at that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I would invite the Defence both to come up with suggestions and also, if possible, respond to what the Prosecution has said until now. And I would also like to stress that sometimes things can even be said better with a few words than with a lot of words. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I noted while Mr. Ierace was speaking, he started at 1308, simply to say that he took 22 per cent of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't quite know, Mr. President, whether I heard well, because you told me -- I never heard a single Defence attorney say that whatever was asked by the Defence was irrelevant or almost irrelevant. If we wish to have efficient meetings, then we don't go into an examination of what has been said or not said. The Defence poses questions that it is entitled to pose in full respect of the Tribunal and the parties, and it will continue to do so. If the Prosecution exceeds its limits, the Defence cannot be asked to spend much less time. It is constrained by the position of the Prosecution. I will give you one example. We were addressed with the problem of exhibits coming from the Prosecution. We received some 1.000 pages. It's only a few weeks ago, and there wasn't a single page. And this is an example of coherent work. A single page that could have been translated into English for the Chamber and for other jurists who don't speak Serbian. One page, we saved time. We spent maybe 15 minutes explaining what it was all about, though it could have been avoided. It is not possible for such a small team as ours to do all this. The Prosecution has five people in the courtroom, and what I would like to say is the following: We asked, in order to facilitate things, to have an assistant with us. We can follow the transcript, listen to the translations, consult each other in the course of the hearings and, at the same time, ask the assistant to look for documents and prepare copies in time. This right was denied us. So if we don't have the instruments to work with, we cannot do our work properly. And finally, regarding the relevance of questions, there are certain questions by the Prosecution when one wonders why they're being put, but it's not up to the Defence to ask. If those questions are put, then the Defence has to respond. Finally, when the Defence calls its own witnesses, it will do so briefly and concisely. It will be questioning them briefly and concisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not hear any response as to the proposals made by the Prosecution, the first proposal being that witnesses would be allowed to read out part of the statement which is not really contested; the second proposal that leading questions, as they have been used this morning, were allowed; and the third one, to interrupt witnesses if they do not strictly keep to the question but are dwelling in their answers. Could you please respond to these proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first point, I will respond, but after consulting with my colleague, who is the lead counsel in this case. Thank you very much. And I would just add that when we suggested, I think it was yesterday, for the actual statement to be tendered, from which an excerpt was cited, it seemed to be a great problem. So there are contradictions on the part of the Prosecution, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, the first suggestion is not acceptable, Mr. President. One of the reasons being the following, if I may explain it to you. Thank you. We spoke at length about Witness Ashton, and you saw that if we had to take some time in questioning him, it was because this witness said, following a question from the Prosecution, that some photos were taken in July. We quickly looked through the chronology and we saw that that was not possible, that there was a contradiction there. Of course, I would never say that that witness was lying, because I have not been educated in that way. I thought that I was quite clear in highlighting those contradictions. Perhaps this was not quite clear -- it would not have been clear to the Court and the parties if we hadn't examined him in such detail, and so this is an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but if I would just, for the sake of debate, suggest to the parties -- well, let's say to have the witnesses read their curriculum vitae, so whether they worked in a certain place, whether they owned a certain company, whether they did it before the conflict, whether they did it during the conflict, would these be sections acceptable to the Defence to be read? And then, of course, there's a right of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I do have to confer with my colleague. Thank you. My personal response would have been yes immediately, and of both of us again, it is yes, because this is only logical. We have just one observation to make, that is: If it should be useful if the Defence to specify such-and-such a point, it can come back to that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So as a principle, the Defence would not oppose against being read by the witness - and I perhaps ask to confirm whether this was correct or not - parts of his earlier statement, especially those parts which are identified - and perhaps the Defence or the Prosecution could confer on that - those parts that are not contested by the other party. There's always a possibility to come back to that in cross-examination. If the Defence would think that at a certain part of examination-in-chief would give a different impression from just reading out the statement, of course they could indicate this to the Prosecution, and if there's any -- so that's the first proposal --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to be very clear about this. We quite agree with the reading of the C.V., or the particulars regarding the witness. On the other hand, however, it is quite clear that if we have to agree beforehand as to what is contested or not, that would be an enormous amount of work for the Prosecution and the Defence outside the courtroom which could become an obstacle for our preparations. I'm just raising the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. You'll understand, on the other hand, that I'm mainly looking at the long-term effects. It might save you some weeks of holiday this summer. So apart from that, I also can imagine that we have been confronted with evidence again and again about Mojmilo hill, Mount Trebevic. Could the parties, in one way or another, try to find out whether there's common understanding as to what were, even it's not very precise, but what was certainly Serbian-held parts and what were ABiH-held parts so that we don't have to come back again and again to hear every witness tell us that Trebevic -- Mount Trebevic was Serbian held. Of course, I do understand if there would have been any shift, but I'm trying to find a bit of common ground. Would there be a possibility to achieve more than has been done in the pre-trial stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, allow me to reply. I believe that there are exhibits established by the UN people, the SFOR people, which clearly show where the confrontation lines were, so this kind of document could be a basis for the two parties. That is quite clear. On the other hand, however, if a witness -- let's take the example we had today, and says my hospital was or was not close to such-and-such a military installation, then one has to ask him once again where the front line was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the view of the Defence, but of course, to hear 50, 60, or 70 times that Mount Trebevic was not ABiH controlled, that might be a bit -- perhaps I'm mistaken, but that's what my understanding is until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand well, Mr. President, but one of the solutions would be to follow in the footsteps of your predecessor, who told the Prosecutor give us much less documents and much fewer witnesses. So I think one way of proceeding would be to cut on the number of witnesses. Then you wouldn't hear a hundred times that Mount Trebevic was in the hands of this side or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as far as I understand, it could be compromised between the parties, so I think it's the two parties who caused the situation. The second proposal as far as the leading questions are concerned, is there any opposition against that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, I have to confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the uncontested area. That's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I manage not to object.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I should like to determine what question we're discussing now, actually. If we are discussing something that has not been challenged and is not contested, I can inform the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution and the Defence, a year ago, discussed the facts which were offered by the Prosecution, and they were 96 proposals in all, that the Defence stated its views with respect to those proposals and that both the Prosecution and Defence sent to the Trial Chamber the discussion they had with respect to the facts that they had agreed upon, not in dispute, and we're rather surprised that my learned colleagues, regardless of the cooperation which we have had, which was very proper this past year, should, at a Status Conference of this kind, which we have not prepared for, are proposing that we talk about something that has been -- is in dispute and is not in dispute. All I can say as the Defence is that the Defence is always ready to sit down to the negotiating table with its colleagues and to discuss these serious matters, the serious matters contained in the indictment. We're always ready to discuss them. But let me repeat: What we said was not in dispute. We signed that together and sent it to the -- and forwarded it to the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, what I was trying to find out is whether there would be any other areas which I do not find yet in the documents sent to the Chamber on which these parties could compromise. Leading questions, I do understand that your position is that it might not be easy to find out what is not in dispute or that it is clear, but I did not hear any objection as such against leading questions in an area which is not contested. Then the third is the interruption of witnesses. I would say this has happened several times by now. I think both parties, especially the Prosecution, has done so. I've heard no objections, so I would like to continue this -- to practice this way. Let me then finally, because we've still got a few minutes left, I first of all would like to thank the parties for their suggestions and for their positive reactions to what we asked. Let me, before going into a bit more detail, first tell you - and this is a very practical issue - that the Chamber felt that sitting in the afternoon was not the most pleasant time, and since in the month of March we would sit almost always from a quarter past 2.00 until 7.00 in the evening in the afternoon, we asked the Court management to give some mornings as well. This is accepted, provisionally, which means that in week 9, starting on the 25th of February, we would sit in the morning from 9.00 to 1.45. In week 10, started the 4th of March, we would sit in the afternoon, started from 2.15 until 7.00 in the evening. Week 11, a morning session again, 9.00 to 1.45. Week 12, which begins on the 18th of March, afternoon sessions, 2.15 until 7.00 p.m. Week 13, started the 25th of March, from 9.00 to 1.45. I further inform you that this Chamber intends to stay in recess in the week of the 29th of April until the 3rd of May, and in the week from the 10th until the 14th of June. If we then keep in mind that we need approximately one week for holidays - I'm talking about the Easter Monday and these kind of UN holidays, and we might lose somewhere one week by unforeseen circumstances - then we would have available to us, until the beginning of July, approximately 20 weeks. Since we are sitting, generally speaking, 18 hours a week, that would be 360 hours. Since we've used already some 40 hours, that would be 400 hours until the beginning of July. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 1765 to 1766. This Chamber feels that, especially with the very constructive proposals made, that it would be possible to complete the presentation of the Prosecution case by the beginning of July. We therefore also invite the Prosecution, I would say, to draft a scenario which would result in completing the Prosecution's case by the beginning of July. If the Prosecution, by reconsidering the necessity of all witnesses, by reconsidering the areas to be covered by the examination-in-chief, by speeding up, according to your own suggestions, the examination-in-chief, if you have all reconsidered this, you wind up with a new list of witnesses and perhaps even new time estimates. If you could draft an emergency scenario which would make it possible to end the case presentation by the Prosecution at the beginning of July, we then could evaluate at the beginning of each week where we stand, and that would make it better possible for this Chamber to see whether there's any necessity of giving strict orders or that it can continue to leave it up to the parties to secure a fair trial, of course, but also a trial without undue delay, the case presentation within reasonable time. So we invite the Defence to do this. I'm not going to comment on what happened during the first couple of weeks. I could give a few examples as well. I think it would be wiser at this moment to refrain from that. I nevertheless would give you, as a guidance, that it's the opinion of this Chamber that cross-examination could be limited, and if the time spent by the Prosecution would not be fully taken in

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: as such, I think. The Chamber also agrees with the Prosecution that Rule 90, and I'm specifically referring to - and it's not upon the request of the Prosecution that we pay attention to it, but it was written down already in my notes - that Rule 90(H), and especially the second element of it, where the limits of cross-examination are considered, should be kept very strictly by the Defence. As far as relevance is concerned, just allow me to give you one example, the matter of whether a clinic or a hospital was private or public or State Hospital, asked about relevance, finally the Defence has told us that it was the name of the hospital that was of importance. They asked for the name, and that was it. I checked it. The name was mentioned seven times before during cross-examination. So I also would like to pay attention to the relevance. I think if we could proceed this way, we might work together closely and see whether the case presentation of the Prosecution could be completed by the beginning of July. It may be clear that, in order to keep control and not to be confronted with a situation where this Chamber would have to give decisions in a situation of a great dilemma, we want to avoid that situation, so therefore the Prosecution is invited to give to the Chamber their new schedule, witnesses, time estimates. You can take a couple of days in order to achieve that, and then we'll be in a position to evaluate every week and to see whether it's necessary to give any orders or that we can leave it to the parties, which this Chamber would prefer. I think it's now already past a quarter to 2.00. We have to stop. If there are any additional observations to be made, you can do it during one of the next few days. So we stay in recess -- we adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

cross-examination by the Defence, this would not in any way harm the trial
--- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
